text:
Good job AMD, but now you have the same problem Nvidia did early in the DLSS cycle. It's locked to only 9070 GPUs, can't be run on previous generations or other vendors' hardware as it's no longer open source, and can't even be upgraded to on the majority of games that support FSR because they're below 3.1. With ever decreasing market share AMD is going to have to incentivize developers to use it moving forward until they can get market share back up to 20%+.

Meanwhile DLSS4 can be utilized by literally every RTX owner going back 4 generations and applied to every game that's ever utilized DLSS.

It's great that they finally have the quality where it needs to be, but this will do nothing to sway the Nvidia buyer that already has access to superior upscaling across a magnitude more games without buying a new generation. Hopefully they'll back port it later so I can use it on my AMD card (Hopefully open source it too) but when it has far less AI capabilities I don't expect it will be performant enough to use it, which is the whole reason you use upscaling to begin with.

This feels a lot like when Nvidia spit in 30 series owners' faces with the introduction of frame gen. Imagine how an XTX owner feels right now. "Not for you unless you buy new!"

text:
I honestly think FSR will surpass DLSS soon, its already so close after 1 attempt and the biggest reason is that AMD took their time

the way AI upscaling works is by first using a temporal upscaler like FSR 3 and then feeding that output to a machine learning model to further improve the image quality, AMD has had so long to perfect pure temporal upscaling that while their AI is not as good as Nvidias, their base input is better, anyone whos tried using NIS (Nvidia Image scaling) knows its far behind FSR 3, NIS is the base temporal upscaler DLSS is based on, but Nvidias AI is so good that it can take a poor input and make a good output

once AMD can catch up on the AI front, their input is better then DLSS, meaning a better image overall then even DLSS 4

text:
In Red Dead Redemption 2 DLSS Transformer model (310.2.1) does not render sparks from the fire (it is also the same for DLAA mode forced via DLSSTweaks 0.310.0.0a). In case of the CNN model (3.8.10) - the sparks are present, like in native TAA mode. It's definitely a problem in model training. Apparently, the Transformer model considers small particles as artifacts and removes them (although when overlapping with smoke - it still draws them, but with terrible halos). I wonder how FSR4 will behave in this situation.
Definitely the Transformer model is not an ideal of image quality and its problems should be identified.
Especially when it deletes details completely instead of improving them - that is unacceptable, regardless of some clarity improvements.
Unfortunately Youtube comments doesn't allow links to screenshots. You can install the Particles mod for RDR2 which increases the particle count to make the process more visual, sit by the fire and spin the camera.

text:
a major problem is also availability. DLSS is in hundreds of games (like well over 500 games iirc), which can all use DLSS 4 Transformer model - if its not integrated natively, it can be activated through the Nvidia app and if its not available in there, you can use DLSS Swapper. FSR 4 on the other hand is in way less games.  And iirc FSR 4 can be used only in FSR 3/3.1 titles (right? or was it ONLY FSR 3.1 titles even?) and there are only around 70 or something of those. 

So besides the fact that FSR 4 seems to be significantly behind the DLSS 4 Transformer model, it is available in WAY less games and that difference in numbers will never be erased, since new games basically always release with either DLSS or DLSS AND FSR. author: @MLWJ1993

text:
To be honest, the difference between FSR 3.1 and FSR 4 was not unexpected, it was a deliberate decision AMD made not to go down the AI path for an upscaler when they first released FSR. They wanted a platform and architecture agnostic upscaler. I think people forget that massive caveat when doing side by side comparisons. Now they have decided to engage in the AI upscaling, likely due to pressure from reviewers, Intel and Nvidia, we are seeing with FSR 4 what they were capable of. As someone who works with AI/ML models, there is also nothing transformative about the transformer model, these models have existed for a while now and as Nvidia have shown, it is likely one of the options for the evolution of upscaling technologies. But there are other models and it will be interesting to see how AMD and Intel evolve their upscalers.

I think the only draw back of FSR 4 is lack of backwards support for RDNA 3 GPUs, which also have AI accelerators, especially as they are not releasing high end cards for RDNA 4 to encourage upgrading from RDNA 3 unless in the mid-range. This is a huge oversight given DLSS 4's transformer model works even on RTX 20-series cards; even if you don't want to enable ray reconstruction. However, paired with AMD's frame generation, ironically, where available, there is extra life added to the RTX 20-series GPUs for ray reconstruction with the transformer model. 

Great work from AMD, but HUGE oversight regarding FSR 4's backwards compatibility with RDNA 3 given no high end RDNA 4.

text: From my pov, what AMD is doing on paper with FSR2 is great. If devs implement FSR2 directly into their engine, it would be more optimized and can be tailored to each game requirement. It is the ideal thing where devs have all control on stuff that can affect the visual. Unfortunately reality kicks in. Most devs doesn't care about actually optimizing their FSR2 implementation. They basically just use DLSS2/3 piping and plug it to FSR2. FSR2 doesn't sit closer to the game engine and basically just becoming a different version of DLSS. They relied on the graphics vendor to improve the upscaling which obviously with FSR2 means there usually no improvement after the initial implementation because they don't want to spend their time to improve it.

@jamminen74  it's really quite simple. If your performance enhancing tool decreases quality compared to native. And doesn't give you much increased performance, what's the point.

DLSS and FSR never gave insane performance gains anyway even with the older models which gave substantially more performance than the new FSR4 and transformer model. 
Going from native to DLSS quality drastically decreases texture quality and motion clarity and adds ghosting and artifacting. Yet in most games DLSS quality is only about a performance gain from 60fps to 80fps. Now with the transformer model or FSR4 we're not even getting that much performance increase. 

We've been too focused on seeing how the new upscalers compare quality wise to the old ones that we lost sight of if they're even worth using in the first place.

I just find it funny how this video doesn't compare to native at all. 
Native is a great option. Especially if literally half your performance gains from making your game look worse with upscaling are lost by increasing the quality of the upscaling to FSR4 or transformer model.

Maybe you don't care about quality. I personally hate using DLSS3, I'd rather wait until I can run a game native than run with DLSS. But for years everyone gaslight me into believing DLSS looked no different, it's amazing. Then the second DLSS4 comes out every youtuber releases a video saying how the entire screen turns into a blur with even small amounts of camera movement when using DLSS3 and now DLSS4 is better..... I've been saying that for years and everyone said I'm being ridiculous and just upscale everything already. 

You want to see FSR8 and DLSS9 in action today... Turn off DLSS. 
You hate the idea now and just saying I'm an "upscale hater". But you'll be raving about how good the quality I'm enjoying today is in 10 years time when upscalers don't degrade your quality nearly as much as they do now, for way less performance gains than they used to.

author: @jamminen74

text:
@jamminen74  I'm not saying they are bad to use. Ultimately, they are the only way some graphics cards can run certain graphical features. 

I'm not going to knock the technology that is the only reason I can play games with path tracing in real time. 

But it's important to acknowledge their limitations and what you're sacrificing. 

As I said, before DLSS4 came out I saw so many people online and content creators praising DLSS3 for things that as soon as DLSS4 came out they trashed DLSS3 for and acted like DLSS3 is a severely compromised way to play the game.. and I've been called crazy for saying that all this time. 

DLSS and FSR are fine, we're used to them by now. But don't kid yourself believing that they don't still have all the same blurry issues as TAA but arguably worse if you turn the internal resolution down. 

I just think we need more comparisons to native, or even SSAA is all. We're being conditioned to accept blurry motion and low texture quality. When that's the whole point of 1440p+ monitors, higher video settings and 1440p+ capable cards, is increased clarity. And we're losing sight of that by not even comparing these technologies to native anymore, not in terms of performance or visual quality. Or the fact that the entire point of DLSS and FSR is increased performance in exchange for decreased clarity. Yet these new models decrease performance quite drastically which was their whole point for even existing. 
Makes me wonder if there's even much point to these technologies anymore if they aren't even performant anymore. Or if you'd just be better off using a 1440p monitor instead of a 4k one and running native res or 1440p SSAA in games you have the headroom for it in.

Absolutely, and next. The key is to make Modular still viable, making Modular emulate the Unified Architecture. The main challenge in emulating a unified memory architecture with modular components is overcoming the bandwidth and latency limitations of traditional interconnects like PCIe. Emulating a unified memory architecture with modular components could significantly improve performance in data-intensive applications, reducing bottlenecks and enabling smoother and more responsive experiences. The pursuit of emulating unified memory could drive innovation in both hardware and software, leading to new technologies and architectures that benefit consumers.

This is AMD's strength, 2018-2020, the unified system. But now it's time to emulate it.

text: Don't celebrate just yet, they have to follow this up with something even better next time. It will take more than this to move the needle in any meaningful way in terms of costs and quality of the products. Nvidia could get away with keeping their prices the same if they maintain a similar or better advantage in the next generation, or if they improve their raw rasterization to true generational uplifts. The thing we should be thinking about right now is that Nvidia clearly put a lot of effort into their AI tech this generation, that sets them up to focus on other things for the next generation. Wat happens if they make some improvements there but then pivot and also make huge improvements to their rasterization and native performance, then the upscaling and frame generation are just bonuses on top? Well, that just means once again that Nvidia can get away with charging what they're charging because AMD probably wouldn't have caught up yet. Until AMD can compete against a current gen high end Nvidia card for performance and upscaling quality, I don't think we're going to see much change in the costs of anything.
